numbers.headline: In a national US survey, 344 of 530 adults ever hooked on weed had already got free.
numbers.mirror: You think being hooked on weed is just who you are now.
numbers.counted: people who had ever been hooked on weed

basis.design: a national US survey, face-to-face interviews, one snapshot
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the doctors' older checklist for being hooked on weed (3 or more of 7 signs within a year)
basis.n: 530 adults ever hooked on weed (of 43,093 surveyed); 344 of them were free by the interview
basis.measured: Whether the signs of being hooked had finally stopped and never come back, as people recalled it. Free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using.

numbers.caveat: 65% is 344 of 530 as a plain head count; the survey's own adjusted figure could differ a little. Some of the other 186 may still get free later. The authors say people may over-report getting free, and people in prison or hospital weren't asked. Weed was weaker in 2001 than today.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.

numbers.headline: 97% of Americans ever hooked on weed are projected to get free of it at some point in their lives.
numbers.mirror: You think you've smoked too long to ever get free.
numbers.counted: people who had ever been hooked on weed

basis.design: a national US survey, face-to-face interviews; ages recalled, then a statistical model projects the share over a whole life
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the doctors' older checklist for being hooked on weed
basis.n: 530 adults ever hooked on weed (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as recalled. From these ages the model projects the share free by the end of life. A projected 66% were free within 10 years.

numbers.caveat: A model, not a head count: 344 of the 530 were free when asked. People in prison or hospital weren't surveyed, so the authors say the true share is probably lower. Free means no signs of being hooked, not never using. Men got free more slowly than women.
numbers.weak: A projection from recalled ages that likely runs high; the same paper's projections for each ethnic group run from 82% to 96%, all below 97%.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.

numbers.headline: Americans who beat a weed problem were about 29, on average, when it ended.
numbers.mirror: You're in your twenties and fear you'll never stop.
numbers.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 217 of the 2,002 people surveyed named weed as their main problem (the survey adjusts its counts to match the US population)
basis.measured: Age when the problem ended, as people remembered it. On average they started weekly use at about 17 and the problem lasted about 12 years.

numbers.caveat: An average age, not a cut-off: the likely range for the average is about 26 to 31. It counts only people who said they got free. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
numbers.weak: The problem was self-defined and most in this survey were never diagnosed, so milder cases are mixed in with addiction.

numbers.headline: Of daily users changing on their own, 85% tried cutting down; only 8% later had a month without weed.
numbers.mirror: You keep cutting down instead of stopping, and it never lasts.

basis.design: daily phone check-ins for 3 months, then a survey at 6 months
basis.who: daily or near-daily weed users (5+ days a week) planning to stop or cut down on their own, not in treatment; half men, average age 32. 75% met the checklist for a weed problem, mild cases included.
basis.measured: Each day: weed use, and whether they were trying to stop or cut down. 85% tried cutting down at some point and 46% tried stopping. At 6 months, 8% had not used weed in the last month.

numbers.caveat: Volunteers paid for daily calls, not a random sample. Almost every try to stop or cut down lasted under a week. Only 6% sought treatment. numbers.headline: Off weed at the end of treatment: 27 in 100 given a THC medicine, vs 26 in 100 given dummy pills.

basis.where: mostly USA (29 trials), also Australia, Israel, Canada and the UK

numbers.headline: At the last check-up, 23 in 100 people given talk therapy were off weed, vs 12 in 100 given little or none.
numbers.mirror: You wonder if therapy is worth it after failing alone.
numbers.counted: people in therapy trials for a weed problem

basis.who: adults with a weed problem (cannabis use disorder), treated as outpatients or in the community
basis.n: the 8 trials that reported how many were off weed (the review's 23 trials had 4,045 people; the head count behind these averages is not stated)
basis.where: 15 trials in the USA; others in Australia, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, Brazil and Ireland
basis.measured: Off weed means no use in the month before the check-up, mostly confirmed by urine or hair tests. Therapy was about 7 sessions over 12 weeks; little or none means minimal or no treatment, such as waiting for treatment later. The review sums up the treated as about a quarter off weed at the last check-up.

numbers.caveat: Averages across trials, not one head count, and the last check-up came at different times. In the 6 trials that could be combined (1,166 people), more were off weed at about 4 months with therapy than without, but the review calls that evidence weak. No kind of therapy clearly worked at 9 months or later. More than 4 sessions over more than a month did better than shorter therapy; adding rewards for clean urine tests helped in 5 of 6 trials.
numbers.weak: Averages across trials, with no head count stated.

ref.cite: Gates PJ, Sabioni P, Copeland J, Le Foll B, Gowing L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for cannabis use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016(5):CD005336. Discussion, 'Point-prevalence and continuous abstinence'.

numbers.headline: In a weed treatment trial, those who had stopped rated life quality 12 points higher, out of 100, than those still smoking.

beliefs.limiting: I’ve smoked for years. I’m stuck.
beliefs.counterpart: Most people hooked on weed get free in the end. I’m doing it now.
beliefs.test: Pick one day this week and live it as a man already getting free: no weed from waking to bed, with the evening planned before it starts. Before you sleep, name one thing the day gave you.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 344 of 530 people ever hooked on weed were already free when asked. 97.2% are projected to get free in their lifetime; half within about 6 years. “Free” means no signs of being hooked.

beliefs.limiting: I can’t handle quitting. Last time I barely lasted three days.
beliefs.counterpart: It’s a few hard weeks, not forever. I’ve got through hard weeks before.
beliefs.test: Tonight, put your first smoke off by one hour and spend that hour on something physical: a walk, a workout, a cold shower. When the hour is up, compare how hard it was with how hard you expected.
beliefs.proof: Weed withdrawal usually lasts up to 3 weeks; poor sleep can last longer. In 49 people hooked on weed and paid to stay off for two weeks, harm to daily life was fairly mild on average, very high for some.

beliefs.limiting: Day 10, I feel fine. Now I can handle it.
beliefs.counterpart: Feeling fine means the withdrawal is over, not that I’m in control again.
beliefs.test: On a day you feel fine, when “just one” comes up, say “I don’t smoke” and leave the room for ten minutes. Then check whether the pull passed on its own.
beliefs.proof: Of 82 people treated for weed dependence who got 2+ weeks off, 71% smoked again within 6 months, and 71% of those went back to 4+ days a week. Early slips led back more often.

beliefs.limiting: Weed is the only thing that gets me to sleep.
beliefs.counterpart: Weed knocks me out. It doesn’t give me good sleep. Some rough weeks buy my real sleep back.
beliefs.test: Pick one night this week with nothing early the next day. Skip the evening smoke, keep your bedtime, phone outside the bedroom. Expect to take longer to fall asleep. In the morning, check two things: did you dream, and how clear is your head?
beliefs.proof: Of 302 adults hooked on weed starting treatment, 69% slept poorly. In 53 young frequent users paid to stop, sleep got worse in week 1, better in week 2, and was back to its old level by week 4.

do: Keep smoking as usual for a few days while you log. No cutting down yet.
Allow it. No guilt while you log: you’re investigating, not failing.
Write down what weed does for you: sleep, boredom, anxiety, fun.
Before each smoke, note the time, where you are and what you want from it.
After it, note whether it gave you that, and for how long.
Each thing weed does for you is a belief to test. Start with the beliefs above.
plan.changeNote: Task G and owner-lens finding: 'Start with the table above' now 'Start with the beliefs above' (they are cards, not a table). Order now allow, log, then test, as his step reads; 'Each one' made explicit after the move; 'while you do this' now 'while you log'. No action removed.

do: Sleep: same wake-up time every day, no screens in bed.
Evenings: plan the first 14 in advance: gym, cooking, a friend, a game.
Anxiety: a walk or a hard workout when it spikes.
Boredom: two things that keep your hands busy, set up before the date.
Keep the ritual, swap the joint: same break, same balcony, tea or a walk instead.
For each need on your step 1 list, write one swap. 80% of the effect is enough.

proof.text: Of 25 long-time daily smokers who quit without treatment for a year or more, the most common things that kept them off were avoiding situations where they smoked, a changed routine and new interests. A small group.

ref.cite: Ellingstad TP, Sobell LC, Sobell MB, Eickleberry L, Golden CJ (2006). Self-change: a pathway to cannabis abuse resolution. Addictive Behaviors 31(3):519-30.
ref.quote: The most common reported maintenance factors were avoidance of situations in which cannabis was used, changes in lifestyle, and the development of non-cannabis-related interests.

do: Pick a date a few days to a few weeks out. Put it in your calendar. Smoke as usual until then.
Throw out the stash, grinder and papers. Delete the dealer’s number.
Expect the first two weeks to be the hardest.
For three months, weed is the one thing. No new diet, no new life plan.
Every day without weed is a complete success. Mark it off.
If you slip, you’re not back at zero. Go back through steps 1–3, find what the slip gave you, and set a new date.

proof.text: In 18 heavy users who stopped, symptoms usually started on days 1–3, peaked on days 2–6, and most lasted 4–14 days.

ref.cite: Budney AJ, Moore BA, Vandrey RG, Hughes JR (2003). The time course and significance of cannabis withdrawal. Journal of Abnormal Psychology 112(3):393-402.
ref.quote: Onset typically occurred between Days 1-3, peak effects between Days 2-6, and most effects lasted 4-14 days.

do: When someone offers, say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m taking a break”.
Notice the “I can moderate now” thought, and treat it as a symptom.
When the urge hits, say “there is a craving”, not “I need to smoke”. Then watch it.
Rate it 0 to 10 and watch it drop. You don’t have to fight it or obey it.
Expect “just one” once you feel fine. Decide your answer now, not at the party.
Tell the people you smoke with that you’ve stopped. Not paused: stopped.

proof.text: In a 12-week treatment trial of 302 adults hooked on weed, craving started lowest and fell within weeks for 41%, and started moderate and fell over time for another 38%. Everyone was paid for clean tests.

ref.cite: Alias-Ferri M, Flesaker M, Gray K, Tomko R, McPherson S, Korthuis PT, et al. (2026). Longitudinal craving profiles in cannabis use disorder: a latent class growth analysis of the ACCENT (CTN-0053) trial. Drug and Alcohol Dependence 285:113208.
ref.quote: A four-class solution provided the best fit: low craving (41%), moderate-decreasing craving (38%), moderate-stable craving (11%), and high craving (10%).

do: Look for CBT with motivation sessions, over a month or more.
Ask about programmes that reward clean tests.
Help is a tool, not a verdict. Use what works, drop what doesn’t.
Free and quick: one friend who quit, an online quit group, a Marijuana Anonymous meeting.
A few meetings can be enough. You don’t sign up for life.

proof.text: In trials for a weed problem, 23 in 100 people given talk therapy were off weed at the last check-up, vs 12 in 100 given little or none.

ref.cite: Gates PJ, Sabioni P, Copeland J, Le Foll B, Gowing L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for cannabis use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016(5):CD005336.
ref.quote: to 23% at follow‐up of longer than four months. In contrast, an average of 12% of those in control conditions reported PPA at final follow‐up.

card.headline: 63% of Americans who beat a weed problem were off weed completely when asked; the other 37% still used some.
card.mirror: You hope you can keep smoking now and then, just not daily.
card.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 217 people whose main problem was weed (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Whether people were currently not using weed at all when surveyed, among those who said the problem was over. The paper gives no time window for this figure; its figure for being off every substance used the past 90 days.

card.caveat: It shows which way people who got free went, not which way works better. They judged for themselves that the problem was over. It doesn't say how much the other 37% still use, or how many tried to keep using and slid back. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
card.weak: Counts only people who got free, so it cannot compare how often stopping and cutting down fail; the problem was self-defined.
